claim: The Sae2/CtIP protein is required for efficient processing of DNA double-strand breaks that initiate homologous recombination in eukaryotic cells.
source: The Sae2/CtIP protein is required for efficient processing of DNA double-strand breaks that initiate homologous recombination in eukaryotic cells.
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract summarizing established knowledge about Sae2/CtIP function.

claim: Sae2/CtIP is important for survival of single-stranded Top1-induced lesions.
source: Sae2/CtIP is also important for survival of single-stranded Top1-induced lesions and CtIP is known to associate directly with transcription-associated complexes in mammalian cells.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations in the introduction and by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: CtIP is known to associate directly with transcription-associated complexes in mammalian cells.
source: Sae2/CtIP is also important for survival of single-stranded Top1-induced lesions and CtIP is known to associate directly with transcription-associated complexes in mammalian cells.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract.

claim: Depletion of Sae2/CtIP promotes the accumulation of stalled RNA polymerase at sites of highly expressed genes.
source: Here we investigate the role of Sae2/CtIP at single-strand lesions in budding yeast and in human cells and find that depletion of Sae2/CtIP promotes the accumulation of stalled RNA polymerase and RNA-DNA hybrids at sites of highly expressed genes.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3B.

claim: Depletion of Sae2/CtIP promotes the accumulation of RNA-DNA hybrids at sites of highly expressed genes.
source: Here we investigate the role of Sae2/CtIP at single-strand lesions in budding yeast and in human cells and find that depletion of Sae2/CtIP promotes the accumulation of stalled RNA polymerase and RNA-DNA hybrids at sites of highly expressed genes.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E, Figure 5, and Figure 6.

claim: Overexpression of the RNA-DNA helicase Senataxin suppresses DNA damage sensitivity in Sae2/CtIP-deficient cells.
source: Overexpression of the RNA-DNA helicase Senataxin suppresses DNA damage sensitivity and R-loop accumulation in Sae2/CtIP-deficient cells, and a catalytic mutant of CtIP fails to complement this sensitivity, indicating a role for CtIP nuclease activity in the repair process.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A, Figure 1B, and Figure 4A.

claim: Overexpression of the RNA-DNA helicase Senataxin suppresses R-loop accumulation in Sae2/CtIP-deficient cells.
source: Overexpression of the RNA-DNA helicase Senataxin suppresses DNA damage sensitivity and R-loop accumulation in Sae2/CtIP-deficient cells, and a catalytic mutant of CtIP fails to complement this sensitivity, indicating a role for CtIP nuclease activity in the repair process.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E and Figure 4D.

claim: A catalytic mutant of CtIP fails to complement DNA damage sensitivity in CtIP-deficient cells.
source: Overexpression of the RNA-DNA helicase Senataxin suppresses DNA damage sensitivity and R-loop accumulation in Sae2/CtIP-deficient cells, and a catalytic mutant of CtIP fails to complement this sensitivity, indicating a role for CtIP nuclease activity in the repair process.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: CtIP nuclease activity plays a role in the repair process of transcription-associated lesions.
source: Overexpression of the RNA-DNA helicase Senataxin suppresses DNA damage sensitivity and R-loop accumulation in Sae2/CtIP-deficient cells, and a catalytic mutant of CtIP fails to complement this sensitivity, indicating a role for CtIP nuclease activity in the repair process.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that a catalytic mutant fails to complement the deficiency.

claim: R-loop processing by 5' flap endonucleases is a necessary step in the stabilization and removal of nascent R-loop initiating structures in eukaryotic cells.
source: Based on this evidence, we propose that R-loop processing by 5' flap endonucleases is a necessary step in the stabilization and removal of nascent R-loop initiating structures in eukaryotic cells.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Double-strand breaks in DNA are lethal lesions in eukaryotic cells.
source: Double-strand breaks in DNA are known to be lethal lesions in eukaryotic cells, and can be an important source of genomic instability during oncogenic transformation because of the possibility of misrepair, translocations, and rearrangements that initiate from these lesions (Aparicio et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Double-strand breaks can be an important source of genomic instability during oncogenic transformation.
source: Double-strand breaks in DNA are known to be lethal lesions in eukaryotic cells, and can be an important source of genomic instability during oncogenic transformation because of the possibility of misrepair, translocations, and rearrangements that initiate from these lesions (Aparicio et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Phosphorylated Sae2/CtIP promotes the activity of the Mre11 nuclease in the MRX(N) complex.
source: Phosphorylated Sae2/CtIP promotes the activity of the Mre11 nuclease in the Mre11/Rad50/Xrs2(Nbs1)(MRX(N)) complex, which initiates the trimming of the DNA end on the 5ʹ strand (Cannavo and Cejka, 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The Mre11 nuclease in the MRX(N) complex initiates the trimming of the DNA end on the 5' strand.
source: Phosphorylated Sae2/CtIP promotes the activity of the Mre11 nuclease in the Mre11/Rad50/Xrs2(Nbs1)(MRX(N)) complex, which initiates the trimming of the DNA end on the 5ʹ strand (Cannavo and Cejka, 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Sae2/CtIP and MRX(N) promote the removal of the Ku heterodimer.
source: Sae2/CtIP and MRX(N) promote the removal of the Ku heterodimer, which acts as a block to resection during non-homologous end joining (Cannavo and Cejka, 2014; Reginato et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2017) and also recruit the long-range 5ʹ to 3ʹ nucleases Exo1 and Dna2 which do extensive processing of the ends (Cejka et al., 2010; Myler et al., 2016; Nicolette et al., 2010; Niu et al., 2010; Shim et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The Ku heterodimer acts as a block to resection during non-homologous end joining.
source: Sae2/CtIP and MRX(N) promote the removal of the Ku heterodimer, which acts as a block to resection during non-homologous end joining (Cannavo and Cejka, 2014; Reginato et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2017) and also recruit the long-range 5ʹ to 3ʹ nucleases Exo1 and Dna2 which do extensive processing of the ends (Cejka et al., 2010; Myler et al., 2016; Nicolette et al., 2010; Niu et al., 2010; Shim et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Sae2/CtIP and MRX(N) recruit the long-range 5' to 3' nucleases Exo1 and Dna2.
source: Sae2/CtIP and MRX(N) promote the removal of the Ku heterodimer, which acts as a block to resection during non-homologous end joining (Cannavo and Cejka, 2014; Reginato et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2017) and also recruit the long-range 5ʹ to 3ʹ nucleases Exo1 and Dna2 which do extensive processing of the ends (Cejka et al., 2010; Myler et al., 2016; Nicolette et al., 2010; Niu et al., 2010; Shim et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Exo1 and Dna2 do extensive processing of DNA ends.
source: Sae2/CtIP and MRX(N) promote the removal of the Ku heterodimer, which acts as a block to resection during non-homologous end joining (Cannavo and Cejka, 2014; Reginato et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2017) and also recruit the long-range 5ʹ to 3ʹ nucleases Exo1 and Dna2 which do extensive processing of the ends (Cejka et al., 2010; Myler et al., 2016; Nicolette et al., 2010; Niu et al., 2010; Shim et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Sae2/CtIP possesses intrinsic nuclease activity that is important for the processing of breaks.
source: In addition to the activities of Sae2/CtIP that promote MRX(N) functions, the protein has also been shown to possess intrinsic nuclease activity that is important for the processing of breaks, particularly those formed in the context of protein lesions, radiation-induced DNA damage, or camptothecin (CPT) damage during S phase (Symington, 2016; Chanut et al., 2016; Makharashvili et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Nuclease-deficient CtIP fails to complement human cells deficient in CtIP for survival of radiation-induced DNA damage.
source: Nuclease-deficient CtIP fails to complement human cells deficient in CtIP for survival of radiation-induced DNA damage while homologous recombination at restriction enzyme-induced break sites is comparable to wild-type-complemented cells (Makharashvili et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Homologous recombination at restriction enzyme-induced break sites is comparable to wild-type in cells complemented with nuclease-deficient CtIP.
source: Nuclease-deficient CtIP fails to complement human cells deficient in CtIP for survival of radiation-induced DNA damage while homologous recombination at restriction enzyme-induced break sites is comparable to wild-type-complemented cells (Makharashvili et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Eukaryotic cells lacking Sae2 or CtIP are hypersensitive to topoisomerase one (Top1) poisons such as CPT.
source: Eukaryotic cells lacking Sae2 or CtIP were also observed years ago to be hypersensitive to topoisomerase one (Top1) poisons such as CPT (Deng et al., 2005; Sartori et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Top1 bound to CPT is stalled in its catalytic cycle in a covalent tyrosine 3' linkage with DNA, creating a protein-linked DNA strand adjacent to a 5' nick.
source: Top1 bound to CPT is stalled in its catalytic cycle in a covalent tyrosine 3ʹ linkage with DNA, creating a protein-linked DNA strand adjacent to a 5ʹ nick (Pommier, 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Top1 is highly active at sites of ongoing transcription due to the need for the release of topological stress.
source: Importantly, Top1 is highly active at sites of ongoing transcription due to the need for the release of topological stress in front of and behind the RNA polymerase (Liu and Wang, 1987; Pommier et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 1988).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: MRX(N) complexes and Sae2/CtIP are essential for the removal of 5' Spo11 conjugates during meiosis.
source: Considering that MRX(N) complexes as well as Sae2/CtIP are essential for the removal of 5ʹ Spo11 conjugates during meiosis (McKee and Kleckner, 1997; Neale et al., 2005; Prinz et al., 1997) coincident with their role in 5ʹ strand processing, it is surprising that Sae2/CtIP-deficient cells exhibit such sensitivity to 3ʹ single-strand lesions, and the mechanistic role that Sae2/CtIP plays at these lesions is currently unknown.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Transcription can play a major role in promoting genomic instability by forming stalled transcription complexes and RNA-DNA hybrids in the genome.
source: In recent years, it has become clear that transcription can play a major role in promoting genomic instability by forming stalled transcription complexes and RNA-DNA hybrids in the genome (Sollier and Cimprich, 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Stable annealing of nascent RNA with the DNA template strand can occur at sites of stalled RNA polymerase complexes.
source: Stable annealing of nascent RNA with the DNA template strand can occur at sites of stalled RNA polymerase complexes, and the 'R-loops' formed in this way can block replication as well as other DNA transactions (Santos-Pereira and Aguilera, 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: R-loops can block replication as well as other DNA transactions.
source: Stable annealing of nascent RNA with the DNA template strand can occur at sites of stalled RNA polymerase complexes, and the 'R-loops' formed in this way can block replication as well as other DNA transactions (Santos-Pereira and Aguilera, 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: R-loops can lead to single-strand and double-strand breaks in DNA that provide recombinogenic intermediates for misrepair events.
source: A wealth of evidence accumulated recently suggests that these events can lead to single-strand and double-strand breaks in DNA that provide recombinogenic intermediates for misrepair events (Costantino and Koshland, 2015; Hamperl et al., 2017; Huertas and Aguilera, 2003).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The Sen1 protein in budding yeast regulates termination of RNA polymerase II transcription.
source: The Sen1 protein in budding yeast has been shown to regulate many aspects of RNA biology, including termination of RNA polymerase II transcription, 3′ end processing of mRNA, and dissociation of RNA-DNA hybrids (Mischo et al., 2011; Steinmetz et al., 2006; Finkel et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The Sen1 protein in budding yeast regulates 3' end processing of mRNA.
source: The Sen1 protein in budding yeast has been shown to regulate many aspects of RNA biology, including termination of RNA polymerase II transcription, 3′ end processing of mRNA, and dissociation of RNA-DNA hybrids (Mischo et al., 2011; Steinmetz et al., 2006; Finkel et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The Sen1 protein in budding yeast regulates dissociation of RNA-DNA hybrids.
source: The Sen1 protein in budding yeast has been shown to regulate many aspects of RNA biology, including termination of RNA polymerase II transcription, 3′ end processing of mRNA, and dissociation of RNA-DNA hybrids (Mischo et al., 2011; Steinmetz et al., 2006; Finkel et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The human ortholog of Sen1, Senataxin, resolves RNA-DNA hybrids.
source: The human ortholog of Sen1, Senataxin, has also been shown to resolve RNA-DNA hybrids (Skourti-Stathaki et al., 2011; Yüce and West, 2013; Cohen et al., 2018) as well as to associate with replication forks to protect fork integrity when traversing transcribed genes (Alzu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Senataxin associates with replication forks to protect fork integrity when traversing transcribed genes.
source: The human ortholog of Sen1, Senataxin, has also been shown to resolve RNA-DNA hybrids (Skourti-Stathaki et al., 2011; Yüce and West, 2013; Cohen et al., 2018) as well as to associate with replication forks to protect fork integrity when traversing transcribed genes (Alzu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Mutations in the gene encoding Senataxin are responsible for the neurodegenerative disorder Ataxia with Oculomotor Apraxia two.
source: Mutations in the gene encoding Senataxin are responsible for the neurodegenerative disorder Ataxia with Oculomotor Apraxia two as well as an early-onset form of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (Groh et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Mutations in the gene encoding Senataxin are responsible for an early-onset form of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.
source: Mutations in the gene encoding Senataxin are responsible for the neurodegenerative disorder Ataxia with Oculomotor Apraxia two as well as an early-onset form of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (Groh et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Overexpression of Sen1 markedly improved survival of the sae2Δ strain to genotoxic agents.
source: We found that overexpression of the termination factor Sen1 markedly improved survival of the sae2Δ strain to genotoxic agents (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: PCF11 improves the survival of yeast strains lacking SAE2 when tested for survival of CPT.
source: We also found that PCF11, a component of the cleavage and polyadenylation complex (CPAC) (Grzechnik et al., 2015; Birse et al., 1998), improves the survival of yeast strains lacking SAE2 when tested for survival of CPT but there was little effect of overexpressing other proteins that also regulate transcription through RNA Pol II including SSU72, RTT103, NRD1, and YSH1 (Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: PCF11 is a component of the cleavage and polyadenylation complex (CPAC).
source: We also found that PCF11, a component of the cleavage and polyadenylation complex (CPAC) (Grzechnik et al., 2015; Birse et al., 1998), improves the survival of yeast strains lacking SAE2 when tested for survival of CPT but there was little effect of overexpressing other proteins that also regulate transcription through RNA Pol II including SSU72, RTT103, NRD1, and YSH1 (Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Overexpression of SSU72, RTT103, NRD1, and YSH1 had little effect on survival of sae2Δ strains.
source: We also found that PCF11, a component of the cleavage and polyadenylation complex (CPAC) (Grzechnik et al., 2015; Birse et al., 1998), improves the survival of yeast strains lacking SAE2 when tested for survival of CPT but there was little effect of overexpressing other proteins that also regulate transcription through RNA Pol II including SSU72, RTT103, NRD1, and YSH1 (Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The ability of Sen1 overexpression to partially alleviate the toxicity of CPT was observed with the Mre11 nuclease-deficient mutant mre11-H125N.
source: The ability of Sen1 overexpression to partially alleviate the toxicity of CPT was also observed with the Mre11 nuclease-deficient mutant mre11-H125N (Moreau et al., 1999) and particularly with the double mutant sae2Δ mre11-H125N (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The ability of Sen1 overexpression to partially alleviate the toxicity of CPT was particularly observed with the double mutant sae2Δ mre11-H125N.
source: The ability of Sen1 overexpression to partially alleviate the toxicity of CPT was also observed with the Mre11 nuclease-deficient mutant mre11-H125N (Moreau et al., 1999) and particularly with the double mutant sae2Δ mre11-H125N (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: A mutation located in the conserved helicase domain of Sen1 (G1747D) reduces the ability of Sen1 to overcome CPT toxicity in the sae2Δ strain.
source: A mutation located in the conserved helicase domain of Sen1 (G1747D) reduces the ability of Sen1 to overcome CPT toxicity in the sae2Δ strain (Figure 1A) but there was no effect of R302W, a mutation reported to block binding to the Rpb1 subunit of RNA Pol II (Chinchilla et al., 2012; Finkel et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The R302W mutation in Sen1 had no effect on CPT toxicity in the sae2Δ strain.
source: A mutation located in the conserved helicase domain of Sen1 (G1747D) reduces the ability of Sen1 to overcome CPT toxicity in the sae2Δ strain (Figure 1A) but there was no effect of R302W, a mutation reported to block binding to the Rpb1 subunit of RNA Pol II (Chinchilla et al., 2012; Finkel et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The R302W mutation in Sen1 blocks binding to the Rpb1 subunit of RNA Pol II.
source: A mutation located in the conserved helicase domain of Sen1 (G1747D) reduces the ability of Sen1 to overcome CPT toxicity in the sae2Δ strain (Figure 1A) but there was no effect of R302W, a mutation reported to block binding to the Rpb1 subunit of RNA Pol II (Chinchilla et al., 2012; Finkel et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The sen1-G1747D mutant is deficient in transcription termination but not in 3' end processing of RNA.
source: The sen1-G1747D mutant is deficient in transcription termination but not in 3′ end processing of RNA (Mischo et al., 2011), thus we conclude that the termination function of the Sen1 enzyme is important for the rescue of CPT sensitivity in sae2Δ strains.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The termination function of the Sen1 enzyme is important for the rescue of CPT sensitivity in sae2Δ strains.
source: The sen1-G1747D mutant is deficient in transcription termination but not in 3′ end processing of RNA (Mischo et al., 2011), thus we conclude that the termination function of the Sen1 enzyme is important for the rescue of CPT sensitivity in sae2Δ strains.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that the G1747D mutant, which is deficient in termination, reduces the ability to rescue CPT sensitivity.

claim: Sen1 overexpression in sae2Δ cells has no effect on the efficiency of resection.
source: In contrast, Sen1 overexpression in sae2Δ cells has no effect on the efficiency of resection (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), as measured in an assay for single-strand annealing (Vaze et al., 2002b) previously shown be dependent on SAE2 due to its importance in DNA end resection (Clerici et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The temperature-sensitive sen1-1 mutant exhibits synthetic lethality in combination with DNA repair mutants mre11, rad50, sgs1, and rad52.
source: In S. cerevisiae, the temperature-sensitive sen1-1 mutant exhibits synthetic lethality in combination with DNA repair mutants mre11, rad50, sgs1, and rad52, indicating a requirement for homologous recombination in the absence of SEN1 function (Mischo et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: A combination of sen1-1 with sae2Δ generates extreme sensitivity to both CPT and MMS.
source: Although the sen1-1 strain is not sensitive to the levels of DNA damaging agents used here, a combination with sae2Δ generates extreme sensitivity to both CPT and MMS (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Deletion of both RNase H1 and H2 in a Δrnh1 Δrnh201 strain generates modest DNA damage sensitivity.
source: Deletion of both RNase H1 and H2 in a Δrnh1 Δrnh201 strain generates modest DNA damage sensitivity as previously shown (Lazzaro et al., 2012; Zimmer and Koshland, 2016; Arudchandran et al., 2000); however, this is further exacerbated by a deletion of SAE2 (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: DNA damage sensitivity in Δrnh1 Δrnh201 strains is further exacerbated by a deletion of SAE2.
source: Deletion of both RNase H1 and H2 in a Δrnh1 Δrnh201 strain generates modest DNA damage sensitivity as previously shown (Lazzaro et al., 2012; Zimmer and Koshland, 2016; Arudchandran et al., 2000); however, this is further exacerbated by a deletion of SAE2 (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Overexpression of RNH1 in a sae2Δ strain from a galactose-inducible promoter partially rescues the strain upon CPT or MMS exposure.
source: Conversely, overexpression of RNH1 in a sae2Δ strain from a galactose-inducible promoter partially rescues the strain upon CPT or MMS exposure (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The sae2Δ strain showed marked sensitivity to CPT specific to exposure in S phase.
source: As expected, the sae2Δ strain showed marked sensitivity to CPT and this was specific to exposure in S phase (Figure 2A), suggesting that movement of replication forks through Top1 DNA damage sites is important for the DNA damage sensitivity.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Movement of replication forks through Top1 DNA damage sites is important for the DNA damage sensitivity in sae2Δ strains.
source: As expected, the sae2Δ strain showed marked sensitivity to CPT and this was specific to exposure in S phase (Figure 2A), suggesting that movement of replication forks through Top1 DNA damage sites is important for the DNA damage sensitivity.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that sensitivity is specific to S phase.

claim: Inhibition of transcription completely alleviated the sensitivity of the sae2Δ strain to CPT, generating wild-type levels of survival.
source: Inhibition of transcription completely alleviated the sensitivity of the sae2Δ strain to CPT, generating wild-type levels of survival (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Sae2 ChIP-seq revealed small peaks of Sae2 enrichment, primarily in the S phase +CPT sample.
source: This analysis revealed small peaks of Sae2 enrichment, primarily in the S phase +CPT sample (176 peaks identified by Model-based Analysis of ChIP-Seq v.2 (MACS2) (Zhang et al., 2008) after removal of overlaps with bead control) (Figure 2C, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C and Supplementary file 2.

claim: Only 45 peaks were identified in S phase in the absence of DNA damage.
source: In contrast, only 45 peaks were identified by this criteria in S phase in the absence of DNA damage.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from ChIP-seq analysis.

claim: The locations of Sae2 binding sites did not correlate with sites of replication origins but were enriched for highly transcribed genes.
source: The locations of the sites enriched with CPT treatment did not correlate with sites of replication origins but were enriched for highly transcribed genes, measuring the overlap between the binding sites and the top 10% of highly transcribed genes (Nagalakshmi et al., 2008; Pelechano et al., 2010; Miura et al., 2008) in comparison to a randomly selected subset (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The enrichment for Sae2 occupancy at sites of high transcription was only observed with cells in S phase, not with the G1 phase cells, and only in cells treated with CPT.
source: The enrichment for Sae2 occupancy at sites of high transcription was only observed with cells in S phase, not with the G1 phase cells, and only in cells treated with CPT.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from ChIP-seq analysis.

claim: Approximately 20% of Sae2 peaks overlap with the sites of RNA-DNA hybrids measured in wild-type yeast cells in a previous study.
source: Approximately 20% (9 of 45 Sae2 peaks in S phase and 36 of 176 Sae2 peaks in S phase with CPT) overlap with the sites of RNA-DNA hybrids measured in wild-type yeast cells in a previous study (Wahba et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of experimental data with a previous study.

claim: sae2Δ cells show approximately 2-fold higher levels of R-loops at the ADH1, ENO2, and FBA1 loci compared to the wild-type strain.
source: We synchronized yeast cells in S phase, exposed the cultures to CPT, and observed approximately 2-fold higher levels of R-loops in sae2Δ cells at the ADH1, ENO2, and FBA1 loci compared to the wild-type strain (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: R-loop signal in sae2Δ cells was reduced with Sen1 expression.
source: This signal was reduced with Sen1 expression and was sensitive to RNaseH treatment in vitro, consistent with this interpretation that R-loops accumulate at these loci in the absence of Sae2.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: R-loop signal in sae2Δ cells was sensitive to RNaseH treatment in vitro.
source: This signal was reduced with Sen1 expression and was sensitive to RNaseH treatment in vitro, consistent with this interpretation that R-loops accumulate at these loci in the absence of Sae2.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: All yeast strains showed very similar levels of RNA Pol II occupancy on the ADH1, ENO2, and FBA1 genes in the absence of DNA damage.
source: All of the strains showed very similar levels of RNA Pol II occupancy on the ADH1, ENO2, and FBA1 genes in the absence of DNA damage (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: When strains were released into S phase in the presence of CPT, the wild-type strain showed an average of 1.5 to 2-fold higher levels of RNA Pol II occupancy.
source: In contrast, when the strains were released into S phase in the presence of CPT, the wild-type strain showed an average of 1.5 to 2-fold higher levels of RNA Pol II occupancy, while sae2Δ strains exhibited 2.5 to 5.5-fold higher levels of polymerase stalling (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: sae2Δ strains exhibited 2.5 to 5.5-fold higher levels of polymerase stalling when released into S phase in the presence of CPT.
source: In contrast, when the strains were released into S phase in the presence of CPT, the wild-type strain showed an average of 1.5 to 2-fold higher levels of RNA Pol II occupancy, while sae2Δ strains exhibited 2.5 to 5.5-fold higher levels of polymerase stalling (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: sae2Δ with Sen1 overexpression showed reduced levels of polymerase occupancy, similar to the wild-type strain with CPT.
source: Importantly, sae2Δ with Sen1 overexpression showed reduced levels of polymerase occupancy, similar to the wild-type strain with CPT.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: CPT-induced RNA Pol II stalling was observed at the PDC1 or NRD1 genes, both known to be dependent on Sen1.
source: We do observe CPT-induced RNA Pol II stalling at the PDC1 or NRD1 genes, both known to be dependent on Sen1 (Alzu et al., 2012; Grzechnik et al., 2015), albeit at a lower level than the genes identified in our Sae2 ChIP experiment.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and citations.

claim: Obvious pausing of RNA Pol II in the absence of Sae2 was induced by CPT at the snoRNA genes SNR13 and SNR5 and the associated gene TRS31.
source: Obvious pausing of RNA Pol II in the absence of Sae2 was also induced by CPT at the snoRNA genes SNR13 and SNR5 and the associated gene TRS31 (Figure 3B), which have been shown to be transcribed by RNA Pol II and exhibit termination read-through, altered RNA Pol II occupancy, and R-loops in the absence of Sen1 function (Steinmetz et al., 2006; Grzechnik et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Sen1 is present at ADH1, ENO2, and FBA1 sites in the absence of SAE2.
source: This showed that Sen1 is present at these sites (ADH1, ENO2, FBA1) in the absence of SAE2 (Figure 3C), thus the binding of the helicase to these sites is Sae2-independent.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The binding of Sen1 to ADH1, ENO2, and FBA1 sites is Sae2-independent.
source: This showed that Sen1 is present at these sites (ADH1, ENO2, FBA1) in the absence of SAE2 (Figure 3C), thus the binding of the helicase to these sites is Sae2-independent.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that Sen1 is present at these sites in the absence of SAE2.

claim: Depletion of CtIP greatly diminishes cell survival in the presence of CPT.
source: As expected, depletion of CtIP greatly diminishes cell survival in the presence of CPT, and re-expression of wild-type CtIP rescues the CPT sensitivity (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Re-expression of wild-type CtIP rescues the CPT sensitivity in CtIP-depleted cells.
source: As expected, depletion of CtIP greatly diminishes cell survival in the presence of CPT, and re-expression of wild-type CtIP rescues the CPT sensitivity (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Overexpression of Senataxin in the CtIP-depleted cells completely rescues the CPT sensitivity.
source: Remarkably, overexpression of Senataxin in the CtIP-depleted cells completely rescues the CPT sensitivity; however, unlike the yeast experiments, no effect of human PCF11 expression was detected (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: No effect of human PCF11 expression was detected on CPT sensitivity in CtIP-depleted cells.
source: Remarkably, overexpression of Senataxin in the CtIP-depleted cells completely rescues the CPT sensitivity; however, unlike the yeast experiments, no effect of human PCF11 expression was detected (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Pre-treatment of cells with DRB partially rescues the CPT sensitivity caused by CtIP deficiency.
source: Indeed, we observe that pre-treatment of the cells with DRB, an inhibitor of RNA polymerase II-dependent RNA synthesis, partially rescues the CPT sensitivity caused by CtIP deficiency (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The recruitment of RNaseH occurs to a higher intensity in CtIP-depleted cells in comparison to cells complemented with wild-type CtIP.
source: Measurement of the accumulation of RNaseHD10R-E48R-mCherry signal over time in these cells showed that the recruitment of RNaseH occurs to a higher intensity in CtIP-depleted cells in comparison to cells complemented with wild-type CtIP, suggesting that higher levels of R-loops are formed in the absence of CtIP (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C and 4D.

claim: Higher levels of R-loops are formed in the absence of CtIP.
source: Measurement of the accumulation of RNaseHD10R-E48R-mCherry signal over time in these cells showed that the recruitment of RNaseH occurs to a higher intensity in CtIP-depleted cells in comparison to cells complemented with wild-type CtIP, suggesting that higher levels of R-loops are formed in the absence of CtIP (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation of higher RNaseH recruitment in CtIP-depleted cells.

claim: With Senataxin expression, the recruitment of RNaseH in the CtIP-depleted cells is reduced to the levels observed in cells expressing wild-type CtIP.
source: We expressed the C-terminal domains of human Senataxin in the CtIP-depleted cells, and measured the levels of laser-induced R-loops by the live cell imaging method. Here also we found that with Senataxin expression, the recruitment of RNaseH in the CtIP-depleted cells is reduced to the levels observed in cells expressing wild-type CtIP (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The NA/HA mutant of CtIP failed to reduce the increased RNaseH recruitment to damage sites that occurs in CtIP-deficient cells.
source: Here we used the N289A/H290A (NA/HA) mutant allele also containing shRNA-resistant mutations to complement CtIP-depleted cells and found that this mutant failed to reduce the increased RNaseH recruitment to damage sites that occurs in CtIP-deficient cells (Figure 4E, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The nuclease activity of CtIP appears to play a role in DNA damage recognition and/or processing that helps to prevent R-loop accumulation in human cells.
source: Thus the nuclease activity of CtIP appears to play a role in DNA damage recognition and/or processing that helps to prevent R-loop accumulation in human cells.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that the nuclease-deficient mutant fails to reduce R-loop accumulation.

claim: Inhibition of transcription rescues the R-loop accumulation phenotype caused by CtIP deficiency.
source: To further test the role of active transcription in R-loop accumulation, we pre-treated cells with 5,6-dichloro-1-beta-D-ribofuranosylbenzimidazole (DRB), a RNA polymerase II inhibitor, and found that inhibition of transcription rescues the R-loop accumulation phenotype caused by CtIP deficiency (Figure 4F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: U2OS cells depleted of Senataxin exhibit increased R-loop formation after laser-induced DNA damage.
source: Indeed, U2OS cells depleted of Senataxin also exhibit increased R-loop formation after laser-induced DNA damage (Figure 4G, Figure 4—figure supplement 1), consistent with previous observations of DNA damage sensitivity in Senataxin mutant cells (Suraweera et al., 2007; Lavin et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: XPG deficient cells accumulate more R-loops after laser induced DNA breaks in comparison to wild-type cells.
source: As expected, we observed that the XPG deficient cells accumulate more R-loops after laser induced DNA breaks in comparison to wild-type cells (Figure 4G, S2G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Concurrent depletion of both CtIP and XPG showed R-loops at levels comparable to wild-type untreated cells.
source: Interestingly, however, concurrent depletion of both CtIP and XPG showed R-loops at levels comparable to wild-type untreated cells (Figure 4H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4H.

claim: R-loops do not form efficiently in the absence of both CtIP and XPG, or they are not recognized efficiently by the RNaseHD10R-E48R-mCherry protein in the absence of both CtIP and XPG.
source: This result suggests that R-loops do not form efficiently in the absence of both CtIP and XPG, or that they are not recognized efficiently by the RNaseHD10R-E48R-mCherry protein in the absence of both CtIP and XPG.
evidence: This is speculation about the interpretation of the observation that R-loops are at wild-type levels in double-depleted cells.

claim: CtIP-depleted U2OS cells show a statistically significant increase in RNaseHD10R-E48R-mCherry fluorescence intensity in all cell cycle phases.
source: Using this procedure, unbound RNaseHD10R-E48R-mCherry protein is removed from the nucleoplasm by detergent extraction, while protein bound to chromatin is retained. This analysis showed a statistically significant increase in RNaseHD10R-E48R-mCherry fluorescence intensity in CtIP-depleted U2OS cells in all cell cycle phases (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The levels of RNaseHD10R-E48R-mCherry fluorescence intensity in CtIP-depleted cells complemented with the nuclease-deficient form of CtIP (NA/HA) are identical to that of CtIP-depleted cells.
source: Similarly, we examined R-loop accumulation in CtIP-depleted cells complemented with the nuclease-deficient form of CtIP (N289A/H290A, NA/HA, Figure 4—figure supplement 2) and found the levels of RNaseHD10R-E48R-mCherry fluorescence intensity identical to that of CtIP-depleted cells (Figure 5B), suggesting that the nuclease activity of CtIP is necessary for R-loop resolution even in cells that are not exposed to exogenous damage.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The nuclease activity of CtIP is necessary for R-loop resolution even in cells that are not exposed to exogenous damage.
source: Similarly, we examined R-loop accumulation in CtIP-depleted cells complemented with the nuclease-deficient form of CtIP (N289A/H290A, NA/HA, Figure 4—figure supplement 2) and found the levels of RNaseHD10R-E48R-mCherry fluorescence intensity identical to that of CtIP-depleted cells (Figure 5B), suggesting that the nuclease activity of CtIP is necessary for R-loop resolution even in cells that are not exposed to exogenous damage.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that the nuclease-deficient mutant shows the same R-loop levels as CtIP-depleted cells.

claim: Undamaged CtIP-depleted or XPG-depleted cells have significantly more R-loops than their wild-type counterparts.
source: We found that undamaged CtIP-depleted or XPG-depleted cells have significantly more R-loops than their wild-type counterparts (Figure 5C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C and 5D.

claim: Concurrent depletion of CtIP and XPG resulted in a lower level of R-loop accumulation.
source: We also observed that concurrent depletion of CtIP and XPG resulted in a lower level of R-loop accumulation (Figure 5D), similar to the result with laser-induced damage (Figure 4H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: CtIP depletion was found to alter 5013 (~16%) of transcripts, with both increases (2,578) and decreases (2,435) observed relative to the control cells.
source: CtIP depletion was found to alter 5013 (~16%) of these transcripts, with both increases (2,578) and decreases (2,435) observed relative to the control cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from RNA-seq analysis.

claim: 1285 transcripts were upregulated upon CPT treatment, and 1158 transcripts were downregulated.
source: We found that there are transcriptional changes associated with CPT exposure in U2OS cells: 1285 transcripts were upregulated upon CPT treatment, and 1158 transcripts were downregulated.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from RNA-seq analysis.

claim: Over 60% of the genes affected by CPT overlap with R-loop prone regions of the genome.
source: Over 60% of the genes affected by CPT (either up or down) overlap with R-loop prone regions of the genome (Ginno et al., 2012) (see 'WT only, - vs +CPT', Figure 5F), whereas less than 40% overlap with DNA-RNA immunoprecipitation (DRIP) positive genes occurs with a randomized control.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Depletion of CtIP has effects on transcription that are correlated with R-loop-prone regions of the genome.
source: A similar analysis of the gene set identified in CtIP-depleted cells compared to normal cells also indicates a higher than expected overlap (~50%), suggesting that depletion of CtIP has effects on transcription that are correlated with R-loop-prone regions of the genome.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation of higher than expected overlap with R-loop-prone regions.

claim: The levels of R-loops increase with doxycycline-induced transcription at the mouse class switch region (Sγ3).
source: We performed DRIP with the S9.6 antibody followed by quantitative PCR for this locus in U2OS cells and found that the levels of R-loops increase with doxycycline-induced transcription, even in wild-type cells (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: A much larger increase in R-loops was found in CtIP-depleted cells at the Sγ3 locus.
source: A much larger increase in R-loops was found in CtIP-depleted cells, however, while the overall levels of transcripts are similar in both cases (Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Higher levels of RNA-DNA hybrids were observed at the β-actin gene in CtIP-depleted cells in the absence of exogenous DNA damage.
source: We observed higher levels of RNA-DNA hybrids at these regions in CtIP-depleted cells in the absence of exogenous DNA damage, which could be reduced to wild-type levels by overexpression of wild-type RNaseH (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: RNA-DNA hybrids at the β-actin gene in CtIP-depleted cells could be reduced to wild-type levels by overexpression of wild-type RNaseH.
source: We observed higher levels of RNA-DNA hybrids at these regions in CtIP-depleted cells in the absence of exogenous DNA damage, which could be reduced to wild-type levels by overexpression of wild-type RNaseH (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: XPG-depleted cells showed an even higher level of R-loops at the β-actin gene.
source: We also tested XPG-depleted cells and observed an even higher level of R-loops under these conditions (Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Significantly higher levels of R-loops were found in CtIP-depleted cells at the RPL13A gene.
source: We tested three locations throughout the body of the RPL13A gene and found significantly higher levels of R-loops in CtIP-depleted cells which were reduced by overexpression of RNaseH in cells (Figure 6D) or by treatment of genomic DNA with RNaseH in vitro prior to the immunoprecipitation (Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: R-loops at the RPL13A gene in CtIP-depleted cells were reduced by overexpression of RNaseH in cells.
source: We tested three locations throughout the body of the RPL13A gene and found significantly higher levels of R-loops in CtIP-depleted cells which were reduced by overexpression of RNaseH in cells (Figure 6D) or by treatment of genomic DNA with RNaseH in vitro prior to the immunoprecipitation (Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: High levels of R-loops were observed at the RPL13A gene in XPG-depleted cells compared to wild-type.
source: We also observed high levels of R-loops at this gene in XPG-depleted cells compared to wild-type (Figure 6E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: R-loops were approximately 1.5 to 2-fold higher in cells expressing the nuclease-deficient NA/HA allele of CtIP in comparison to cells expressing the wild-type allele.
source: Lastly, the nuclease-deficient NA/HA allele of CtIP was expressed in CtIP-depleted cells, and R-loops were found to be approximately 1.5 to 2-fold higher in these cells in comparison to cells expressing the wild-type allele, similar to our observations in uncomplemented cells (Figure 6F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Depletion of CtIP or XPG increases Senataxin occupancy at the inducible (Sγ3) locus by 3 to 5-fold.
source: Here we asked whether Senataxin is recruited to R-loops in the absence of CtIP or XPG and found that depletion of either factor increases Senataxin occupancy at the inducible (Sγ3) locus (Figure 6G) by 3 to 5-fold, similar to our observations of Sen1 in yeast.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: CtIP depletion led to a significant reduction in the accumulation of DNA breaks after CPT treatment.
source: We found that exposure to CPT generated a marked increase in DNA breaks, and that transcription promotes these breaks, as pretreatment with DRB reduced the levels of breaks by ~75% in wild-type cells (Figure 8A). CtIP depletion led to a significant reduction in the accumulation of DNA breaks after CPT treatment, consistent with the proposed model that CtIP can facilitate the conversion of stalled transcription associated DNA lesions into DNA breaks.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Transcription promotes DNA breaks after CPT exposure.
source: We found that exposure to CPT generated a marked increase in DNA breaks, and that transcription promotes these breaks, as pretreatment with DRB reduced the levels of breaks by ~75% in wild-type cells (Figure 8A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: In cells depleted for XPG there are fewer breaks after CPT treatment.
source: In cells depleted for XPG there are fewer breaks after CPT treatment, and in cells depleted for both proteins, we observed no increase in breaks at all with CPT exposure (Figure 8B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: In cells depleted for both CtIP and XPG, no increase in breaks was observed with CPT exposure.
source: In cells depleted for XPG there are fewer breaks after CPT treatment, and in cells depleted for both proteins, we observed no increase in breaks at all with CPT exposure (Figure 8B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Cells expressing the nuclease-deficient NA/HA CtIP mutant showed a large reduction in breaks formed with CPT exposure.
source: To test this, we also examined breaks by comet assay in cells expressing the nuclease-deficient NA/HA CtIP mutant and found that in this case also, there was a large reduction in breaks formed with CPT exposure, very similar to the uncomplemented cells (Figure 8C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: The level of single-strand breaks on the template strand of the RPL13A gene was reduced by 40% to 50% with depletion of CtIP.
source: Using this procedure, we did observe spontaneous single-strand breaks on the template strand of the RPL13A gene, and the level of breaks was reduced by 40% to 50% with depletion of CtIP, again consistent with the observation that single-strand breaks are reduced in cells lacking CtIP.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: Sae2/CtIP is not only a double-strand break resection factor, but also functions at transcription-associated lesions in eukaryotic cells.
source: These results suggest that Sae2/CtIP is not only a double-strand break resection factor, but also functions at transcription-associated lesions in eukaryotic cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Sen1 acts to remove R-loops from genomic loci.
source: Since the Sen1 helicase acts to remove R-loops from genomic loci, we also tested whether sae2Δ strains show synthetic sensitivity to CPT in combination with deletions of RNase H enzymes which remove ribonucleotides from DNA.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Sen1 function.

claim: Sen1 plays a role downstream of Sae2.
source: Alternatively, it is possible that Sen1 plays a role downstream of Sae2 and that in the absence of Sae2 function, Sen1 catalytic activity is less efficient even though its recruitment to damage sites appears to be unimpeded.
evidence: This is speculation about the relationship between Sen1 and Sae2.

claim: Loss of CtIP is lethal in mammalian cells.
source: In mammalian cells, loss of CtIP is lethal whereas yeast strains lacking SAE2 have no growth deficit in the absence of DNA damage (McKee and Kleckner, 1997; Prinz et al., 1997; Chen et al., 2005; Makharashvili and Paull, 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Yeast strains lacking SAE2 have no growth deficit in the absence of DNA damage.
source: In mammalian cells, loss of CtIP is lethal whereas yeast strains lacking SAE2 have no growth deficit in the absence of DNA damage (McKee and Kleckner, 1997; Prinz et al., 1997; Chen et al., 2005; Makharashvili and Paull, 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: CtIP and Sae2 exhibit an intrinsic endonuclease activity that is specific for 5' flap structures.
source: CtIP and Sae2 exhibit an intrinsic endonuclease activity that is specific for 5ʹ flap structures and can be genetically separated from its ability to stimulate the nuclease of activity of Mre11 (Makharashvili et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2014; Arora et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The endonuclease activity of CtIP/Sae2 can be genetically separated from its ability to stimulate the nuclease activity of Mre11.
source: CtIP and Sae2 exhibit an intrinsic endonuclease activity that is specific for 5ʹ flap structures and can be genetically separated from its ability to stimulate the nuclease of activity of Mre11 (Makharashvili et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2014; Arora et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: XPG is an endonuclease that acts in nucleotide excision repair.
source: Since we also show in this work that R-loop formation in CtIP-depleted cells resembles that of cells depleted of XPG, an endonuclease that also acts in nucleotide excision repair, it is possible that both enzymes target 5ʹ flap structures, of which there are at least two present in every R-loop structure (see model in Figure 7).
evidence: This is established knowledge about XPG function.

claim: Both CtIP and XPG may target 5' flap structures present in R-loop structures.
source: Since we also show in this work that R-loop formation in CtIP-depleted cells resembles that of cells depleted of XPG, an endonuclease that also acts in nucleotide excision repair, it is possible that both enzymes target 5ʹ flap structures, of which there are at least two present in every R-loop structure (see model in Figure 7).
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation that both enzymes have similar effects on R-loop accumulation.

claim: There are at least two 5' flap structures present in every R-loop structure.
source: Since we also show in this work that R-loop formation in CtIP-depleted cells resembles that of cells depleted of XPG, an endonuclease that also acts in nucleotide excision repair, it is possible that both enzymes target 5ʹ flap structures, of which there are at least two present in every R-loop structure (see model in Figure 7).
evidence: This is an inference based on the structure of R-loops.

claim: In the absence of both CtIP and XPG, unprocessed nascent R-loops and/or stalled RNA polymerase complexes accumulate.
source: To explain this finding we propose that, in the absence of both CtIP and XPG, unprocessed nascent R-loops and/or stalled RNA polymerase complexes accumulate (Figure 7).
evidence: This is a proposed model to explain the observation of lower R-loops in double-depleted cells.

claim: Nascent R-loop structures are small and are not efficiently recognized by either the S9.6 antibody or by RNase H due to topological constraints.
source: We propose that, due to the topological constraints on R-loop formation, these nascent R-loop structures are small and are not efficiently recognized by either the S9.6 antibody or by RNase H.
evidence: This is speculation to explain the observation of lower R-loops in double-depleted cells.

claim: A nick in the non-template strand greatly improves the efficiency of stable R-loop formation.
source: The idea that a nascent R-loop is topologically constrained and relatively inaccessible in the absence of strand breaks is consistent with previous work showing that a nick in the non-template strand greatly improves the efficiency of stable R-loop formation, because the non-template strand then does not compete with the RNA for hybridization to the template strand (Roy et al., 2010; Aguilera and Gómez-González, 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Cleavage of one of the DNA strands facilitates removal of the RNA-DNA hybrid by transcription-associated helicases such as Senataxin and/or Aquarius.
source: We propose that cleavage of one of the DNA strands, although seemingly detrimental in its stabilization of the RNA-DNA hybrid, likely facilitates removal of the hybrid by transcription-associated helicases such as Senataxin and/or Aquarius.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental data.

claim: The helicase domain of yeast Sen1 requires single-stranded DNA adjacent to the hybrid for efficient loading prior to unwinding of the annealed RNA.
source: Biochemical characterization of the helicase domain of yeast Sen1 showed that the enzyme requires single-stranded DNA adjacent to the hybrid for efficient loading prior to unwinding of the annealed RNA (Martin-Tumasz and Brow, 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Treatment of chromatin with low levels of the single-strand DNA-specific S1 nuclease greatly improves the yield of R-loops immunoprecipitated by the S9.6 antibody.
source: In addition, a recent study found that treatment of chromatin with low levels of the single-strand DNA-specific S1 nuclease greatly improves the yield of R-loops immunoprecipitated by the S9.6 antibody (Wahba et al., 2016), consistent with this hypothesis.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: R-loops greatly increase the level of genomic instability at locations where they accumulate.
source: One possibility is that double-strand breaks form at sites of transcription-replication collisions, since we know that R-loops greatly increase the level of genomic instability at locations where they accumulate, and double-strand breaks have been implicated in these events (Richard and Manley, 2017; Wickramasinghe and Venkitaraman, 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: R-loops form in human cells at DNA sites adjacent to induced double-strand breaks.
source: Recent work demonstrates that R-loops form in human cells at DNA sites adjacent to induced double-strand breaks and that the Senataxin enzyme promotes their removal as well as Rad51 recruitment and homologous recombination (Cohen et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: A subset of R-loops in yeast induce Rad52-bound double-strand breaks.
source: In addition, a subset of R-loops in yeast were shown to induce Rad52-bound double-strand breaks, with the RNA-DNA hybrid located on one side of the break and resected DNA on the other (Costantino and Koshland, 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Double-strand breaks have been shown to accompany high levels of transcriptional activity and appear to facilitate gene expression.
source: Lastly, double-strand breaks have been shown in some contexts to accompany high levels of transcriptional activity and appear to facilitate gene expression (Madabhushi et al., 2015); in this case TopII was implicated in formation of the breaks, but it is not clear if processing of the breaks occurs at these sites or is important for cell survival.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: CtIP was originally identified as a binding partner of C-terminal Binding Protein (CtBP), a transcriptional co-regulator.
source: CtIP was originally identified as a binding partner of C-terminal Binding Protein (CtBP), a transcriptional co-regulator (Schaeper et al., 1998), and also binds directly to Rb and the tumor suppressor BRCA1 which also has been widely reported to affect transcription and R-loop formation (Monteiro et al., 1996; Scully et al., 1997; Takaoka and Miki, 2018; Yu et al., 1998; Hatchi et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: CtIP binds directly to Rb and the tumor suppressor BRCA1.
source: CtIP was originally identified as a binding partner of C-terminal Binding Protein (CtBP), a transcriptional co-regulator (Schaeper et al., 1998), and also binds directly to Rb and the tumor suppressor BRCA1 which also has been widely reported to affect transcription and R-loop formation (Monteiro et al., 1996; Scully et al., 1997; Takaoka and Miki, 2018; Yu et al., 1998; Hatchi et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: BRCA1 has been widely reported to affect transcription and R-loop formation.
source: CtIP was originally identified as a binding partner of C-terminal Binding Protein (CtBP), a transcriptional co-regulator (Schaeper et al., 1998), and also binds directly to Rb and the tumor suppressor BRCA1 which also has been widely reported to affect transcription and R-loop formation (Monteiro et al., 1996; Scully et al., 1997; Takaoka and Miki, 2018; Yu et al., 1998; Hatchi et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: BRCA1 localizes to a subset of transcription termination regions and regulates levels of RNA-DNA hybrids in human cells.
source: BRCA1 itself has been shown to localize to a subset of transcription termination regions and to regulate levels of RNA-DNA hybrids in human cells (Hatchi et al., 2015; Hill et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: XPG was recently found to be present in a complex with BRCA1 that is important for cellular responses to DNA damage.
source: In addition, XPG was recently found to be present in a complex with BRCA1 that is important for cellular responses to DNA damage that is separate from its roles in excision repair (Trego et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: CtIP has been shown to have important repair functions in G1 phase cells.
source: Lastly, CtIP has been shown to have important repair functions in G1 phase cells (Barton et al., 2014; Biehs et al., 2017; Helmink et al., 2011; Quennet et al., 2011; Yun and Hiom, 2009); it will be important to determine if the R-loop processing functions indicated here play a role in the repair of transcription-associated damage even outside of S phase and whether this accounts for any of the essential functions of CtIP in mammals.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.
